_doc: THE LANES THAT MUST BE ADJUDICATED BY THE GEOMETRY CHECKERS.
Read by scripts/check_geometry_checkers.py (R8). Nothing else consumes it.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS -- and it is the same defect as D1, one level up.
D1 moved the wiring rule from 'the flag appears as text anywhere in the
workflow' to 'the flag appears in a `run:` body in the parse tree'. That is
closer to execution but it is still not execution, and the rule was still
phrased over the EVIDENCE: check_ci_wiring iterated `set(writers) |
set(readers)`, so A JOB CARRYING NEITHER FLAG WAS INVISIBLE. Deleting the
writer and the reconcile line from the Windows job -- seven lines, one
commit -- left the gate, its --self-test, and check_lane_coverage.py ALL
GREEN while the Windows seat quietly stopped adjudicating anything. That is
the seat that most needs the guarantee: `swift test` is macOS-only in CI, so
Windows already sees only the Rust arm, and Seam 1 is the whole reason it can
referee the checkers at all.
A rule phrased over what it FINDS cannot notice an absence. So the
obligation is written down HERE, as data, and the gate iterates THIS FILE --
not the jobs it happens to discover. Adding or dropping a lane is then a
deliberate, reviewable act: an edit to this file with a sentence attached,
rather than an emergent consequence of an edit to CI.
A LANE IS A (PLATFORM, LANGUAGE) PAIR, keyed 'platform:language'. Platform is
the runner family the job runs on (windows / macos / linux); language is a
member of cross_language_algorithms.LANGUAGES, and the gate validates the key
against that module so a typo cannot invent a lane nothing can satisfy.
WHAT THE GATE PROVES FOR EACH ROW HERE -- five clauses, all of them about
EXECUTION rather than about the presence of text:
1. some job on that platform RUNS the runner with that language in --lang,
writes a --checker-report, and READS it back with --reconcile in the
same job, at the same path (D1's pairing rule, kept, now per lane);
2. neither that job nor either of those two steps carries an `if:` that
could skip it -- unless this row declares the exact condition in
`permitted_if` and says why;
3. neither that job nor either of those two steps carries
`continue-on-error` -- a step whose failure is ignored is not a check;
4. its `needs:` chain is satisfiable -- every dependency exists, none of
them is itself conditional (a skipped dependency skips this job, so an
`if:` three jobs upstream silently un-adjudicates this lane), and the
chain has no cycle;
5. neither command's exit status is discarded by the shell -- no `|| true`,
no `&&` chain that swallows it under `bash -e`.
BOTH DIRECTIONS, as R1 taught. A lane CI adjudicates that is NOT declared
here also reds: an undeclared lane means this file has gone stale, and a
registry that under-declares is exactly the hole the iteration fix closed.
The same applies to `permitted_if`: declared for a job that carries no `if:`,
it is a STALE excuse and reds. `swift:dropdown` asserted a missing feature
for months after JasSwift shipped it, and on 2026-07-29 a seat read that row,
believed it, and set out to build what already existed.
TO ADD A LANE: add the row with a `reason` saying what it buys that the
other rows do not, wire the job, and raise `MIN_DECLARED_LANES` in
check_geometry_checkers.py in the SAME commit. The floor is exact, not slack
-- a floor with slack is a floor with a hole exactly the size of the slack.
TO DROP A LANE: delete the row and lower the floor, in a commit whose message
says which platform stops being refereed and why that is acceptable. That
sentence is the entire mechanism; nothing here can stop someone who means it,
and nothing here should try.

windows:rust.reason: THE LANE THIS FILE WAS WRITTEN FOR. The Windows seat has no Swift toolchain, so it legitimately requests one lane -- which makes it the lane most easily lost, because losing it changes no comparison count anywhere. It is also the only platform that can see the encoding, newline and separator classes (11 of 24 invocations failed on its first day and not one was a content defect), so a Windows box that stops adjudicating geometry is a referee that reports coverage it no longer has. Seam 1 exists precisely so this box can rule in full: one Python predicate, no second toolchain.

permitted_if.why: Declared for the Windows lane's judging STEPS, isolated by P1.5. The condition is false only when the run is CANCELLED, and a cancelled run publishes no verdict -- it is not a green build over an unadjudicated lane, which is what R8 exists to forbid. It STRICTLY REDUCES the unadjudicated set: before P1.5 every step carried GitHub's implicit `if: success()`, so this writer step was SKIPPED on every run where any earlier step went red -- and measured at 5095060d it WAS skipped, along with two other judging steps, behind a step-17 failure. Eight of the last ten runs skipped 7-9 steps that way. So the set shrinks from 'any run with an earlier red step' to 'runs a human cancelled'. `always()` is deliberately not used: an operator who cancels means it.

macos:rust.reason: The reference arm of the BLOCKING cross-language job. Every checker verdict on macOS is computed against this lane's roundtrip output, so if it stops being adjudicated the swift arm has nothing to disagree with and the equivalence claim degrades to a single-port oracle run without saying so.

permitted_if.why: Declared for the `cross-language` job's condition, added by P1.4. The condition is FALSE ONLY WHEN THE RUN IS CANCELLED, and a cancelled run publishes no verdict at all -- it is not a green build over an unadjudicated lane, which is the outcome this rule exists to forbid. Crucially the condition STRICTLY REDUCES the set of runs where this lane goes unadjudicated. Before it, `cross-language` carried NO `if:` and declared `needs: [rust, swift]`, so it was SKIPPED on every run where either dependency went red -- and a skipped job renders as 'not applicable' while the build stays green, which is precisely an unadjudicated lane under a green build. Measured: run 31114155047 at 5095060d, where the macOS `rust` job died in cargo's own bookkeeping and the prime-directive gate did not run at all. So the set shrinks from 'any run with a red dependency' to 'runs a human deliberately cancelled'. `always()` would shrink it further and is deliberately NOT used: an operator who cancels a run means it, and forcing adjudication through a cancellation would be the opposite defect -- a verdict nobody asked for on a tree nobody finished testing.

macos:swift.reason: The only lane in CI that adjudicates the Swift port's geometry at all -- `swift test` is macOS-only here, so no other platform can carry it. One SKIP_LANG_ALGO entry, or a `--lang` edited down from rust,swift to rust, empties it; R5's reconcile catches that from inside a run, and this row catches the CI edit that stops the run from ever requesting it.
